Cavalieri era discípulo de Galileo y lla: Cavalieri was a pupil of Galileo and called his slices indivisibles. His method raised a considerable row, because it treated a volume as a sum of infinitely many surfaces with no thickness, and to many mathematicians of the day that seemed simply illegitimate. They were partly right: the reasoning was not soundly founded and paradoxes could be built with it. But it worked, and worked so well that it opened the way to integral calculus, which arrived half a century later and gave it the foundations it lacked.

La relación entre el cono y el cilindro: The relation between the cone and the cylinder — one third — is what gives a funnel, a conical glass or a heap of sand the capacity they have, and it is used daily by anyone sizing silos, tanks and aggregate on site. La respuesta es un principio que enunció: The answer is a principle stated by the Italian Bonaventura Cavalieri around 1635, and it can be put in a picture: imagine the two solids cut into extremely thin horizontal slices. Las fórmulas de volumen se recuerdan muc: Volume formulas are far easier to remember grouped into families than one by one. Solids with two equal bases — prisms and cylinders — are “area of the base times height”, and nothing more. Those ending in a point — pyramids and cones — are exactly one third of that, and that third is no accident: three equal pyramids fill exactly a prism of the same base and height. The sphere stands apart and has a story of its own.
